question: The Commission has approved billions of euros of compensation for Germany for the early closure of its lignite mines and power stations. Meanwhile, these stations have been reactivated in recent years under the pretext of securing the electricity supply during the energy crisis. This means that German providers receive public money for their ‘coal exit’ while continuing to burn it in practice.

This approach raises serious questions about the credibility of EU climate policy and about the fair treatment of Member States. While stricter requirements and restrictions are being imposed in many countries, Germany, the EU’s largest economy, is receiving special treatment as it still gains subsidies while prolonging its coal operations.
This not only negatively impacts the competitiveness of other countries but also undermines trust in the Commission itself for accepting such contradictions. In light of the above: 1.
How does the Commission justify granting billions of euros in compensation to Germany for the closure of power plants that have been reactivated?
Does the Commission not recognise that these actions create blatant inequality in relation to other Member States, which have to bear the costs of the transition without similar advantages?
How does the Commission intend to rebuild trust in its own climate and energy policies, given that it accepts obvious contradictions and double standards in the case of Germany?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.1.2026) In 2016, the Commission approved a measure for the closure of lignite-fired power plants in case SA.42536. Plants in the scope of this measure were mothballed for four years, before they were planned to shut down permanently. Payments under this measure were scheduled annually to compensate for forgone profits due to the mothballing.

In 2022, following the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine, Germany decided to transfer some of these mothballed plants to a temporary reserve with the view to temporarily allow those plants to return to the market, to be on stand-by and ready to be activated to the extent needed in the event of natural gas shortages. The Commission approved this latter measure in case SA.

103662 pursuant to Article 107(3)(b) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to remedy a serious disturbance in the German economy. This measure was limited until 31 March 2024 and the Commission assessed specifically in that decision that there is no overlap in compensation with the measure for the closure of lignite-fired power plants, given that the eligible costs are different.
Furthermore, the Commission approved several German measures concerning the early closure of lignite power plants. These plants were or will be closed permanently at the agreed date.
